homes.heading: ## Check the tradition's own rules before asking for a picture of it
paragraphs: RE is full of things a camera can be pointed at - a church, a mosque, a festival meal, a sacred text, a person praying - and the referent test in `preferences.md` → Lesson Designer visual-need boundary applies here as in any subject. What is specific to RE is that some traditions place limits on what may be depicted, and those limits are the tradition's, not a matter of taste. Christian art depicts Jesus freely, so a nativity, a crucifix or a Bible illustration is ordinary teaching material. Islam does not depict Muhammad, and no lesson may request a picture of him or of any prophet (every lesson's rule, no picture of the Prophet Muhammad, is in `preferences.md` → Lesson Designer visual-need boundary); teach through the mosque, the Qur'an, calligraphy, the practice or the community instead. Where you are unsure whether a tradition depicts a figure, request the place, object, text or practice rather than the figure, which teaches the same thing and cannot offend the people being taught about.

homes.heading: ### Lesson Designer visual-need boundary
paragraphs: **Show the class the thing the slide is talking about.** The question to ask of every slide is `does this name something that exists in the world?` - a church, a carol service, a Bible, a food, a coin, a place, a building, an object, a person doing something. When it does, the class should be able to see it while the teacher explains. That picture is what a child looks at while you talk, what you point at, what they hook their own experience on to, and what they ask an unplanned question about. It earns its place on that alone, and nothing has to be decided from it.

The test this replaces is `could a child work the learning out from this picture?`, and it is the wrong test because nothing else on a Teach slide is worked out either. `Christians believe Jesus is God's Son` is told to a class, not deduced by them; a photograph of a packed church at Christmas is told to them in the same way. Refusing the picture because it proves nothing holds it to a standard the sentence beside it never sits, and the subjects where it bites are the ones whose content is belief, feeling, rule or relationship rather than an observable fact. A Year 4 RE lesson on what Christmas means reached a class with a nativity, a carol service and a Bible all available and none of them requested, on the reasoning that meaning cannot be inferred from the appearance of a celebration. True, and beside the point: the child was not being asked to infer anything.

**A person the lesson invents counts as something in the world, and is the hole in that question.** `Does this name something that exists in the world?` gets the answer no for Nadia and Grace, because they are made up, and the slide that quotes them ends up with nothing to look at. That is backwards: an invented person needs showing more than a real one does, not less, because showing them is the only thing that makes a child treat the words as somebody's rather than as an exercise. A Year 4 RE deck put two children's reasons for singing carols on the board as two text cards, with no faces and with the carol-singing photograph it had already sourced sitting unused on four other slides. So when a beat puts a person in front of the class, it owes the class that person: a portrait and a bubble (`slide-speech-and-characters.md` owns how), and the lesson's relevant photograph where one exists. The same test then does its ordinary work on what those people are talking about - carols, a nativity, a tree - and normally finds the picture already in the lesson.

**When the slide names nothing in the world, no picture is wanted, and most decks will rightly have several such slides.** A slide handling the lesson's own business has no referent to show: here is your task, here are the success criteria, here is what we noticed on the slide before. A picture there is decoration sitting where attention should be, and this section is not a quota. The boundary against the paragraph above is whether a person is present in the beat or merely referred back to: two children whose words are on this slide are present, and a line recalling what the class concluded about them yesterday is not. The other limits below hold unchanged and still win where they apply: a picture that hands the child the answer is refused, a tool the engine draws is drawn rather than photographed, and text is the right teaching object when the text is what children are studying.
**Islam does not depict the Prophet Muhammad, and no lesson may request a picture of him.**

**Foundation subject Teach and task-framing slides earn meaningful visual support.** In PSHE, RE, History, Geography and Science, slides that present categories, locations, comparisons, sequences, or the task children are about to investigate should use meaningful visual differentiation when it improves understanding rather than defaulting to plain text columns. The visual treatment may be a labelled diagram, photograph, map, timeline, source, object, shape, icon, emoji or another representation that fits the learning; it does not need to give every individual item its own picture. Text can be the teaching object when the text itself is what children are studying, and a separate picture should not be forced where it adds nothing. The test is which representation teaches the content best, not whether a written description contains enough facts to answer. When children compare objects through their appearance or use, make both sides available through the real things, images, diagrams or another faithful representation. Describing the absent object makes children reconstruct it before they can compare; sufficient answer facts do not remove that burden. Name what they will inspect on each side and what you will explain through it. Add text for context or meaning the objects cannot show. Conversely, words are the right evidence when the learning concerns a statement, account, argument or other information a picture cannot establish - but read that as a rule about which medium carries the *evidence*, never as a reason to leave the slide with nothing to look at, because the referent test above is a separate question that a text-led slide still has to answer. A script saying “look at” something needs that thing available in the resource or explicitly available in the classroom. Task-framing slides in particular fail this test often: the question, the success criteria, and any useful visual or teaching object for the real context, with the wider task description living in speaker notes, is enough to set up the task. Children don't need both a paraphrase of the question AND the success criteria on screen — the SC is what tells them what good looks like. What lives in the notes here is the teacher's *framing* of the task — the orientation, the why-it-matters, the longer description of what's ahead. A Teach slide's because is not framing: it is the route, and it is on the board. A task the children actually carry out at this beat is a different thing and stays on the slide: when the beat asks them to write a prediction, the prediction prompt and its sentence stem go on screen, because writing it is something the child *does*, not something the teacher says. The line to hold is framing-in-notes, task-on-slide — trimming the framing keeps the slide a glance, and keeping the task visible keeps it doable when the notes go unread.

**Giving a task its instructions is not launching it.** Before a substantial task, children may need to know why they are doing it now, what they are making, what a good one looks like and how the work will run, and only then the instruction. Those are beats on the board, not framing prose: the why is one line that gives the class something to hold while they look at the model, and **when the task is about a particular case, that line is the case and the question, not a recap of the teaching**. A child looking at a strong answer beside a weak one with no question in mind is looking at writing; a child who has just met Sam and his squash is looking for how to answer about Sam. So the case comes first, on a short slide of its own before the model, carrying who it is, what happened and what they are being asked - and the task slide keeps the case as well, because that is the board they write from. A recap of what the lesson established (`We've found what our agreement needs: joining in, passing, privacy, questions, help`) is the right line only when the product is the class's own work on what they have just built and there is no case to set; where the strong instance already says the chain, the recap is the same thing said worse and goes; what good looks like is an example beside a non-example with the difference named (`Be respectful` tells you nothing to do; `Listen while someone else is speaking` does); the how is the steps in the order children take them (make one, combine your group's, agree ours). **`steps` are stages of work, not the standard said again.** The teacher deleted a whole steps slide from the tooth deck on 18 September 2026 and the lesson lost nothing: `read what happened to Sam` came after two slides showing Sam, `use the four steps on the board, in order` pointed at the criteria panel on the next slide, `write it as sentences, not as a list` was what the two cards above had just shown, and `read it back: does each sentence say what caused the next one?` was the difference line word for word. The test on each step is whether the class would lose anything it cannot already see if that step were deleted. A task whose work is one sustained go, launched with a model and with the criteria visible while children work, usually leaves `steps` empty; stages earn the field when they really happen in an order and the later ones are invisible until the earlier ones are done. A slide that goes straight to `Write one rule` when none of that has been on the board has left the launch in the notes, and a teacher working from the slide sets the task without teaching it. Framing-in-notes still holds for the teacher's spoken orientation; it does not cover a model, a non-example or the steps, which a child needs to see. Slide count follows: one or two short slides before the task slide, each doing less, never the launch crammed on to the instruction. A short beat children can start from its question alone, and a task whose product this lesson has already shown them a good one of, need none of this. Success criteria on the board that already show what a good one looks like (an actual good one, such as a model answer or a good paragraph, never a list of what a good one includes) stand in for the good instance, so the launch keeps its case and steps and needs no second model. **Decide, and say, which the good instance is: a parallel case children transfer from, or a model of this very case that they rehearse.** Both are legitimate and the failure is only ever claiming the second while planning it as the first. A Year 4 history launch showed `Sigurd came because there was not enough farmland at home for him, and the monastery had silver and nobody to fight back` as the strong answer, and the next slide asked `Why did Vikings like Sigurd sail to Britain?`: the first question was answered a minute before children met it, and the design still counted the writing as each child's own explanation. That is the defect - not the model.

**The parallel case** (another ship, another family) keeps the writing as evidence, and costs transfer: the child holds the shape and changes the content. Choose it when the writing is the lesson's evidence and the class can carry a structure across cases.

**The same case** gives children a complete good one of exactly what they are about to make, which is what a class most often needs and what the teacher asked for on 18 September 2026: `it gives them an example of actually how to do it, what it looks like ... its not on the board when theyre practising, so its all them`. It costs the writing's status as evidence, and two things then have to be true. The design says in `unlocks` and in the answer's acceptance condition that this beat is supported rehearsal. And a later stage - the worksheet, the ending, a fresh case - carries the evidence of what each child can do unaided. A lesson that cannot point at that stage has no evidence and must use the parallel case instead.

Watch for the parallel case that is parallel in name only. Toffees sucked on the way home and squash sipped all afternoon are the same science, and a Year 4 will still spend the first minute of the task talking about toffee; a difference the lesson has not taught (sticky against sipped) is a difference children cannot reason across, so it is friction rather than transfer.

**The good instance is shown, and only the difference is said.** The pair is three separate things - the good instance, the weak one, and the one line naming what makes the good one good - and the board keeps them separate: two cards side by side, a tick on the good one, a cross and red on the weak one, the line underneath. That is the `strong-and-weak` template, and it is the one board in the deck that marks its two cards, because it is the one where the teacher is telling the class which is better rather than asking them; a concept-attainment contrast a child decides stays unmarked (`templates.md` → `compare-words`, `triangle-nonexample`). **The instance is whatever the product is**: written work carries words, a labelled diagram carries the diagram, a design carries the sketch, and a launch for a drawn product shows two drawings rather than a sentence about what a good label says. **The difference is one line a child can hold their own work against, not a paragraph about the contrast.** The two cards are already showing it; the line names what the strong instance *does* that the weak one only states, in words a child can answer yes or no to. `Every sentence picks up the thing before it` fails that - picks up what, and how would a child check it? - and the same lesson said it properly two slides later in its own steps: `Each sentence says what caused the next one.` Where the success criteria or the steps already own that sentence, use their words rather than coining a second way of saying it, so the class meets one wording on the example slide, on the steps and on the criteria panel while they write. It is never `the strong one is better`, which every class answers correctly from length alone, and never an abstraction they can agree with and not apply. A Year 4 science launch (18 September 2026) reached the class as a hundred and fifty words in four stacked blocks - thirty-four of recap, the two instances, and forty-six explaining the difference - with no picture and nothing to tell one card from the other.

**The good instance is a piece of work that would meet this lesson's own success criteria, taught words and all.** That launch modelled an explanation that never said `plaque`, while the criteria the same children were then marked against said `write what the germs in the {{plaque}} do with that sugar`: the class was shown a model that would have failed the standard. The validator refuses it now, matching every `{{taught word}}` in the beat's criteria against the model. The reason to want it beyond the mismatch is what a taught word is for - the test of teaching `enamel` is not whether a child can define it but whether they decide for themselves that it is the word they need to explain the decay, and the model is the one place the lesson can show that decision being made. **And the gathering line goes when the instance already carries it**: that recap listed sugar, germs, acid, enamel and the hole, and the strong instance directly under it said the same chain in sentences. The instance is the better of the two.

section.heading: ## Cross-subject use

present.text: - Maths may use variation, counterexamples, systematic search, representation choice and justified method selection. - English may compare effects, justify structural choices or reason from textual evidence. - **Reading comprehension.** Depth = multi-point inference with multiple pieces of evidence; comparing author's choices across two texts; justifying a competing interpretation; evaluating effect. Pupils writing their own greater-depth question on the extract for a peer is a strong closing move. - **Writing.** Depth = manipulating structure for effect (shift in formality, flashback, sentence-length variation for tension); emulating a studied author's structure; drafting then redrafting for precision; justifying choices. The Year 6 TAF links greater-depth writing to evidence of wide reading drawn on independently — prompt the child to emulate a specific author. - **Grammar.** Depth = explaining the effect, not just identifying the feature. "Write three fronted adverbials for the same clause and rank them for impact." "Spot the mistake in this flawed sentence and explain the rule broken." section.heading: # Subject Discipline: Maths

present.text: Maths lessons here rarely fail on accuracy, and they do not fail through rote success either. Rote fluency is a foundation this school deliberately builds, not a weakness to design around. The failure is what happens after the fluency is built: children who can already do it easily just get more examples. The fluency gets built and never spent. Wasted time.

present.text: The gate runs both ways: for a genuinely new repeatable method, children normally need reasonable execution before later selection or reasoning, unless that thinking is inseparable from understanding the mathematics itself, and once they are secure, staying is the failure.

present.text: RE is full of things a camera can be pointed at - a church, a mosque, a festival meal, a sacred text, a person praying - and the referent test in `preferences.md` → Lesson Designer visual-need boundary applies here as in any subject. What is specific to RE is that some traditions place limits on what may be depicted, and those limits are the tradition's, not a matter of taste. Christian art depicts Jesus freely, so a nativity, a crucifix or a Bible illustration is ordinary teaching material. Islam does not depict Muhammad, and no lesson may request a picture of him or of any prophet (every lesson's rule, no picture of the Prophet Muhammad, is in `preferences.md` → Lesson Designer visual-need boundary); teach through the mosque, the Qur'an, calligraphy, the practice or the community instead. Where you are unsure whether a tradition depicts a figure, request the place, object, text or practice rather than the figure, which teaches the same thing and cannot offend the people being taught about.

present.text: **Show the class the thing the slide is talking about.** The question to ask of every slide is `does this name something that exists in the world?` - a church, a carol service, a Bible, a food, a coin, a place, a building, an object, a person doing something. That picture is what a child looks at while you talk, what you point at, what they hook their own experience on to, and what they ask an unplanned question about. It earns its place on that alone, and nothing has to be decided from it.

present.text: The test this replaces is `could a child work the learning out from this picture?`, and it is the wrong test because nothing else on a Teach slide is worked out either. `Christians believe Jesus is God's Son` is told to a class, not deduced by them; a photograph of a packed church at Christmas is told to them in the same way. Refusing the picture because it proves nothing holds it to a standard the sentence beside it never sits, and the subjects where it bites are the ones whose content is belief, feeling, rule or relationship rather than an observable fact. A Year 4 RE lesson on what Christmas means reached a class with a nativity, a carol service and a Bible all available and none of them requested, on the reasoning that meaning cannot be inferred from the appearance of a celebration. True, and beside the point: the child was not being asked to infer anything.

present.text: **A person the lesson invents counts as something in the world, and is the hole in that question.** `Does this name something that exists in the world?` gets the answer no for Nadia and Grace, because they are made up, and the slide that quotes them ends up with nothing to look at. That is backwards: an invented person needs showing more than a real one does, not less, because showing them is the only thing that makes a child treat the words as somebody's rather than as an exercise. A Year 4 RE deck put two children's reasons for singing carols on the board as two text cards, with no faces and with the carol-singing photograph it had already sourced sitting unused on four other slides. So when a beat puts a person in front of the class, it owes the class that person: a portrait and a bubble (`slide-speech-and-characters.md` owns how), and the lesson's relevant photograph where one exists. The same test then does its ordinary work on what those people are talking about - carols, a nativity, a tree - and normally finds the picture already in the lesson.

A picture there is decoration sitting where attention should be, and this section is not a quota. The boundary against the paragraph above is whether a person is present in the beat or merely referred back to: two children whose words are on this slide are present, and a line recalling what the class concluded about them yesterday is not. The other limits below hold unchanged and still win where they apply: a picture that hands the child the answer is refused, a tool the engine draws is drawn rather than photographed, and text is the right teaching object when the text is what children are studying.

rows.outcome: a paragraph of references/preferences.md ### Lesson Designer visual-need boundary, pinned whole

present.text: **Foundation subject Teach and task-framing slides earn meaningful visual support.** In PSHE, RE, History, Geography and Science, slides that present categories, locations, comparisons, sequences, or the task children are about to investigate should use meaningful visual differentiation when it improves understanding rather than defaulting to plain text columns. The visual treatment may be a labelled diagram, photograph, map, timeline, source, object, shape, icon, emoji or another representation that fits the learning; it does not need to give every individual item its own picture. Text can be the teaching object when the text itself is what children are studying, and a separate picture should not be forced where it adds nothing. The test is which representation teaches the content best, not whether a written description contains enough facts to answer. When children compare objects through their appearance or use, make both sides available through the real things, images, diagrams or another faithful representation. Describing the absent object makes children reconstruct it before they can compare; sufficient answer facts do not remove that burden. Name what they will inspect on each side and what you will explain through it. Add text for context or meaning the objects cannot show. Conversely, words are the right evidence when the learning concerns a statement, account, argument or other information a picture cannot establish - but read that as a rule about which medium carries the *evidence*, never as a reason to leave the slide with nothing to look at, because the referent test above is a separate question that a text-led slide still has to answer. A script saying “look at” something needs that thing available in the resource or explicitly available in the classroom. Task-framing slides in particular fail this test often: the question, the success criteria, and any useful visual or teaching object for the real context, with the wider task description living in speaker notes, is enough to set up the task. Children don't need both a paraphrase of the question AND the success criteria on screen — the SC is what tells them what good looks like. What lives in the notes here is the teacher's *framing* of the task — the orientation, the why-it-matters, the longer description of what's ahead. A Teach slide's because is not framing: it is the route, and it is on the board. A task the children actually carry out at this beat is a different thing and stays on the slide: when the beat asks them to write a prediction, the prediction prompt and its sentence stem go on screen, because writing it is something the child *does*, not something the teacher says. The line to hold is framing-in-notes, task-on-slide — trimming the framing keeps the slide a glance, and keeping the task visible keeps it doable when the notes go unread.

present.text: **Giving a task its instructions is not launching it.** Before a substantial task, children may need to know why they are doing it now, what they are making, what a good one looks like and how the work will run, and only then the instruction. Those are beats on the board, not framing prose: the why is one line that gives the class something to hold while they look at the model, and **when the task is about a particular case, that line is the case and the question, not a recap of the teaching**. A child looking at a strong answer beside a weak one with no question in mind is looking at writing; a child who has just met Sam and his squash is looking for how to answer about Sam. So the case comes first, on a short slide of its own before the model, carrying who it is, what happened and what they are being asked - and the task slide keeps the case as well, because that is the board they write from. A recap of what the lesson established (`We've found what our agreement needs: joining in, passing, privacy, questions, help`) is the right line only when the product is the class's own work on what they have just built and there is no case to set; where the strong instance already says the chain, the recap is the same thing said worse and goes; what good looks like is an example beside a non-example with the difference named (`Be respectful` tells you nothing to do; `Listen while someone else is speaking` does); the how is the steps in the order children take them (make one, combine your group's, agree ours). **`steps` are stages of work, not the standard said again.** The teacher deleted a whole steps slide from the tooth deck on 18 September 2026 and the lesson lost nothing: `read what happened to Sam` came after two slides showing Sam, `use the four steps on the board, in order` pointed at the criteria panel on the next slide, `write it as sentences, not as a list` was what the two cards above had just shown, and `read it back: does each sentence say what caused the next one?` was the difference line word for word. The test on each step is whether the class would lose anything it cannot already see if that step were deleted. A task whose work is one sustained go, launched with a model and with the criteria visible while children work, usually leaves `steps` empty; stages earn the field when they really happen in an order and the later ones are invisible until the earlier ones are done. A slide that goes straight to `Write one rule` when none of that has been on the board has left the launch in the notes, and a teacher working from the slide sets the task without teaching it. Framing-in-notes still holds for the teacher's spoken orientation; it does not cover a model, a non-example or the steps, which a child needs to see. Slide count follows: one or two short slides before the task slide, each doing less, never the launch crammed on to the instruction. A short beat children can start from its question alone, and a task whose product this lesson has already shown them a good one of, need none of this. Success criteria on the board that already show what a good one looks like (an actual good one, such as a model answer or a good paragraph, never a list of what a good one includes) stand in for the good instance, so the launch keeps its case and steps and needs no second model. **Decide, and say, which the good instance is: a parallel case children transfer from, or a model of this very case that they rehearse.** Both are legitimate and the failure is only ever claiming the second while planning it as the first. A Year 4 history launch showed `Sigurd came because there was not enough farmland at home for him, and the monastery had silver and nobody to fight back` as the strong answer, and the next slide asked `Why did Vikings like Sigurd sail to Britain?`: the first question was answered a minute before children met it, and the design still counted the writing as each child's own explanation. That is the defect - not the model.

present.text: **The parallel case** (another ship, another family) keeps the writing as evidence, and costs transfer: the child holds the shape and changes the content. Choose it when the writing is the lesson's evidence and the class can carry a structure across cases.

present.text: **The same case** gives children a complete good one of exactly what they are about to make, which is what a class most often needs and what the teacher asked for on 18 September 2026: `it gives them an example of actually how to do it, what it looks like ... its not on the board when theyre practising, so its all them`. It costs the writing's status as evidence, and two things then have to be true. The design says in `unlocks` and in the answer's acceptance condition that this beat is supported rehearsal. And a later stage - the worksheet, the ending, a fresh case - carries the evidence of what each child can do unaided. A lesson that cannot point at that stage has no evidence and must use the parallel case instead.

present.text: Watch for the parallel case that is parallel in name only. Toffees sucked on the way home and squash sipped all afternoon are the same science, and a Year 4 will still spend the first minute of the task talking about toffee; a difference the lesson has not taught (sticky against sipped) is a difference children cannot reason across, so it is friction rather than transfer.

present.text: **The good instance is shown, and only the difference is said.** The pair is three separate things - the good instance, the weak one, and the one line naming what makes the good one good - and the board keeps them separate: two cards side by side, a tick on the good one, a cross and red on the weak one, the line underneath. That is the `strong-and-weak` template, and it is the one board in the deck that marks its two cards, because it is the one where the teacher is telling the class which is better rather than asking them; a concept-attainment contrast a child decides stays unmarked (`templates.md` → `compare-words`, `triangle-nonexample`). **The instance is whatever the product is**: written work carries words, a labelled diagram carries the diagram, a design carries the sketch, and a launch for a drawn product shows two drawings rather than a sentence about what a good label says. **The difference is one line a child can hold their own work against, not a paragraph about the contrast.** The two cards are already showing it; the line names what the strong instance *does* that the weak one only states, in words a child can answer yes or no to. `Every sentence picks up the thing before it` fails that - picks up what, and how would a child check it? - and the same lesson said it properly two slides later in its own steps: `Each sentence says what caused the next one.` Where the success criteria or the steps already own that sentence, use their words rather than coining a second way of saying it, so the class meets one wording on the example slide, on the steps and on the criteria panel while they write. It is never `the strong one is better`, which every class answers correctly from length alone, and never an abstraction they can agree with and not apply. A Year 4 science launch (18 September 2026) reached the class as a hundred and fifty words in four stacked blocks - thirty-four of recap, the two instances, and forty-six explaining the difference - with no picture and nothing to tell one card from the other.

present.text: **The good instance is a piece of work that would meet this lesson's own success criteria, taught words and all.** That launch modelled an explanation that never said `plaque`, while the criteria the same children were then marked against said `write what the germs in the {{plaque}} do with that sugar`: the class was shown a model that would have failed the standard. The validator refuses it now, matching every `{{taught word}}` in the beat's criteria against the model. The reason to want it beyond the mismatch is what a taught word is for - the test of teaching `enamel` is not whether a child can define it but whether they decide for themselves that it is the word they need to explain the decay, and the model is the one place the lesson can show that decision being made. **And the gathering line goes when the instance already carries it**: that recap listed sugar, germs, acid, enamel and the hole, and the strong instance directly under it said the same chain in sentences. The instance is the better of the two.
